newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S., Canada show some flexibility on lumber quota.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada show some flexibility on lumber quota.

text.p: The trade ministers from Canada and the United States said on Friday they were willing to discuss making small changes to the U.S. quota on Canadian lumber exports.

The two countries had been discussing the agreement and talked about "how to fine-tune" the system, said U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky after a news conference on trade talks among Canada, the United States, Japan and the European Union.
"If there's any opportunity for flexibility, then we're quite prepared to talk about it," said Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton.

In a five-year agreement started in April 1996, Canada can export 14.7 billion board feet of lumber a year duty free to the United States. Tariffs of US$50 and US$100 per 1,000 board feet are liable on shipments above that level.

Canada agreed to the quota after years of bickering with the United States over Canada's softwood lumber exports, but Eggleton has made it clear that he hoped to revert to a free market once the five-year quota deal was up.
On Thursday, 20 members of the U.S. House of Representatives unveiled a bill to end the U.S. quota, since the quota pushed up lumber prices and made housing more expensive.
But both Barshefsky and Eggleton said on Friday that the quota system was working well and they were pleased with it so far.
